runs.text: der a todos os do Reino.

lines.note: Continues the preceding page’s Portuguese sentence with “to all those of the kingdom”; the opening der is the physical remainder of a divided word, not a new headword.
Uchinabiku denotes bending or inclining. The Portuguese begins with inclinar-se and dobrar-se; the principal forms are retained in the dictionary’s spelling.

runs.text: como eruas, ramos, &c. com o vento. ¶ Itẽ.

lines.note: The bending is illustrated by herbs and branches moved by wind. The paragraph mark and abbreviated Itẽ introduce a second sense on the next row.

runs.text: Inclinarſe, ou rẽderſe o coração, & võtade de

lines.note: The transferred sense is a person’s heart or will yielding. The nasal abbreviations in rẽderſe and võtade remain unexpanded.
Cocoroga vchinabiqu illustrates the heart inclining or yielding, completing the preceding reference to someone’s heart and will.
Uchinamidagumu means the eyes fill with tears; the Portuguese reflexive verb begins this description and is completed by olhos below.

runs.text: olhos de agoa, ou com lagrimas.

lines.note: The eyes become full of water or tears. Agoa and lagrimas retain the printed historical spelling and accentuation.
Uchinarasu is ringing a bell or making something sound by striking it. The historical -aita form is part of the verb’s stated principal forms.
Completes the explanation of making something sound by striking it; algũa retains its visible abbreviation mark.
The noun uchinarashi denotes a small bell, compared to a batega or metal basin. This is a distinct entry after the verb.
The small bell is struck by Buddhist monks, called Bonzos in the Portuguese gloss; the Portuguese loan designation stays italic.
Uchinasare is the passive expression for being reduced to a certain number of survivors. The visible principal-form punctuation has ru eta without an added comma.

runs.text: em certo numero ſendo os de mais mortos à eſ-

lines.note: The reduction occurs because the remaining people have been killed by the sword. The visibly divided eſ- continues as pada below.
Juushichiki ni uchinasareta gives the example of being reduced to seventeen mounted men; the verb is divided at the printed hyphen.

runs.text: Tornarão ſe em dezaſete de cauallo.

lines.note: Ta completes uchinasareta. The Portuguese states that seventeen horsemen remained; the long ſ in Tornarão ſe is preserved.
Uchinoburu means making something long or extending it. The line ends in a comma after comprida, joining the following alternative gloss.
Caneuo vchinoburu is extending metal by hammering it. The Portuguese Ba is the visible first part of Batendo on the next line, with no supplied hyphen.

runs.text: tendo ferro, ou outro metal estendelo.

lines.note: Tendo completes Batendo: hammering iron or another metal to lengthen it. The printed estendelo is retained without modernizing its orthography.
Vouo vchinoburu means lengthening a cord. The scan supports initial v in vchinoburu and cordão, correcting the OCR’s ychinoburu and condão.
The cord is made longer; the next example concerns postponing unnecessary litigation or petitions. The divided vchi- belongs to vchinobete below.
Nobete voqu completes the postponement expression. Portuguese diferir means defer; the visible f corrects OCR diſerir, and petiçoẽs retains its tilde position.
Desneceßarias qualifies the petitions as unnecessary. The scan joins the printed word without the OCR’s space after des and retains its ß-like type.
Uchinobu is stretching out completely. The following example specifies a sleeping posture; the introductory Vt ends with a comma.
Uchinobite nuru means sleeping fully stretched out, exactly the posture described in the Portuguese translation.

runs.text: Moço de caſa, ou de ſeruiço.

lines.note: Uchinomono denotes a household servant or serving boy, as the Portuguese moço de caſa and de ſeruiço specify.
Uchinokuru means removing or pushing something aside. The printed or before afaſtar is retained as an apparent anomaly rather than silently changed to expected ou.

runs.text: mão, ou dando com pao, Catana, &c.

lines.note: Removal can be done with the hand or by striking with a stick or a katana. Catana is the Japanese weapon name embedded in the Portuguese explanation.
Uchinozomu describes arriving at a place, specifically the arrival of troops as the next line explains. The printed ôda retains its circumflex.
A gente de guerra supplies the subject of chegar: a body of soldiers arriving. This short continuation belongs to uchinozomu.
Uchikiru is glossed simply as cutting or killing. The stated past form itta is retained rather than expanded or modernized.
Uchikiseru means dressing or arming another person. The principal form ſuru is retained as printed, and ou- begins outro across the row break.
Yoroiuo totte vchi qixete illustrates taking armour and dressing another in it. The visible separation vchi qixete is preserved; To- begins the Portuguese gerund.

runs.text: mando as armas, & veſtindo as a outro.

lines.note: Mando completes Tomando: taking the arms and putting them on someone else. The pronoun as remains separate from veſtindo as in the print.
The paragraph mark introduces a metaphorical sense: assailing the enemy with a mass of men. Ninjuuo vchiqixete cacaru is the military example; the OCR had omitted the visible paragraph mark.

runs.text: Dar ſobre os inimigos cubrindo os, ou carre-

lines.note: The Portuguese describes falling upon the enemy and covering or overwhelming them. Carre- continues into carregando on the next row.

runs.text: gando com muita gente ſobre elles.

lines.note: Completes carregando: pressing on the enemy with many men. This explains the metaphorical use of the preceding verb.
Uchisamasu is referred to Samasu by the printed Vide cross-reference. The dictionary’s abbreviated principal forms remain in the line.

runs.text: Vchiſauagui, gu, ida. i, Sauagui, gu.

lines.note: Uchisawagu is equated with Sawagu, making noise or commotion. The equivalence marker i, and its neighboring punctuation remain unexpanded.
Uchisou denotes staying very close or attached to someone. Both inflectional long-o marks are circumflexes in the scan; apegado is printed as one word.
Junto a alguem completes the sense of being close beside another person, rather than introducing a new entry.
Uchitsugau is setting an arrow on the bow. The two principal-form long-o marks are carons, contrasting with uchisou above.
Yumito yauo vchitçugǒ combines bow and arrow in the example; Idem sends the reader to the same definition.
Uchitsukena describes presumptuous or heedless behavior. The Portuguese deſa- continues into deſatentada on the next physical row.

Uchitçuqena cotonaredomo begins “although it is presumptuous.” The consonant in -redo- is abraded at its top; the surviving rounded base and concessive construction favor d over the OCR’s c. The chosen reading remains qualified, and the word stays divided at the printed hyphen.
Mo completes the concessive ending; goyǒuo mǒsǒzu expresses the intended request. The Portuguese begins its matching “although it may be” clause.

runs.text: muita liberdade, ou atreuimento pedirei hũa

lines.note: The request may be excessive familiarity or presumption, yet the speaker asks a favor. The scan restores the OCR’s broken wording to muita liberdade and final hũa without an invented hyphen.
Merce, ou graça completes the request for a favor or grace. This is the object of pedirei on the preceding row.

Uchitçuqeni is the adverb corresponding to uchitçuqena. The partly abraded headword is supported by its surviving tç and the adjacent adjective, correcting OCR Vchiaçuqeni. The NINJAL headword index, consulted after the scan reading, corroborates this identification (Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, v202510; NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida; CC BY 4.0; https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html).
Uchitsukuru means fastening something, with the comparison co/mo beginning across the row break. There is no supplied hyphen after the visible co.
The first sense compares fastening with a nail. The paragraph mark introduces another sense involving throwing or striking something against a surface.

runs.text: dando com algũa couſa pegala como barro à pa-

lines.note: The material sticks, as clay does to a wall. The scan gives barro, correcting the OCR’s batro, and the divided pa- continues into parede below.
Rede completes parede, the wall used in the clay example. The short continuation belongs to the preceding gloss.
Uchitsuredatsu is going together in company. The abbreviated nasal in cõpanhia is preserved, as are the principal forms tçu and atta.
Uchitsuzuku means continuing or following successively. The print lists u rather than an editorially supplied qu among its principal forms; that apparent omission is retained.
The succession is immediate, one after another. The separated a pos is the actual historical wording rather than modernized após.
Uchite first means a killer, then a player of games. The paragraph mark distinguishes these two senses of the agent noun.
The games include dice, tables, and Go. Go is a Japanese game name embedded in the Portuguese gloss; Bacuchi starts the Japanese example.
Bacuchi or suguroku no uchite means a dice or board-game player. The alternative marker l is separate from the Japanese wording.
The dictionary adds that the word can sometimes mean a good player. Its Latin aliquando qualifies this supplementary sense.
Uchitodomuru is equated with uchikorosu and glossed “kill.” The Japanese synonym follows i, and is not part of a Portuguese explanatory sentence.
Uchitomuru has the same meaning, as the italic Idem indicates. It is a separate headword and physical row.
Uchitokuru means revealing oneself completely. The Portuguese gloss continues by specifying familiarity and absence of reserve.
Familiarmente and ſem peio describe open, unreserved self-disclosure. The visible i after fam corrects OCR famaliarmente.
Cocoroga vchitoquru illustrates the heart opening freely. The next sense is introduced by the visible abbreviation Itẽ, not the OCR’s truncated It.

runs.text: Desfazerſe de todo, ou derreterſe como cara-

lines.note: A further sense is melting or dissolving completely, compared here to caramelo. The scan supports joined Desfazerſe and derreterſe, correcting the OCR’s split word and extra t.
Melo completes caramelo. Vchitoqete iru introduces the sense of remaining relaxed and at ease, whose Portuguese translation continues below.
The gloss is being very confident and at ease. Deſcanſado has a visible c, correcting OCR deſtanſado.

runs.text: Mostra de roſto que não tem

lines.note: Uchitokegao is an open facial expression that conceals no different feeling in the heart. The line starts that description without naming a separate emotion.
The face and inner feelings agree. Vchitoqega- begins the example with the compound divided over the next physical row.

runs.text: Mostrar no roſto, ou no exterior

lines.note: Uouo ſuru completes the example of showing an open countenance; the Portuguese describes manifesting on one’s face or exterior what is within.

runs.text: tudo o que hum tem no peito.

lines.note: Everything in the breast or heart is outwardly shown. This completes the explanation of the transparent expression in the preceding example.
Uchitoru means killing someone and taking the person’s head. The Portuguese object and possessive phrase finish on the following row.
Lhe a cabeça completes the action of taking the slain person’s head. The continuation is kept as its own physical line.

runs.text: Certo abano redondo que não ſe fecha.

lines.note: Uchiwa names a round fan that does not fold. Fecha is supported by the visible f and the explanation of the fan’s construction, correcting OCR ſecha.

runs.text: Os de dentro dalgũa familia, ou que

lines.note: A separate uchiwa entry denotes members of a household or people under a leader. The Portuguese definition continues into the captain’s dependants below.
Those within a household include people under a captain. The scan gives eſtão, correcting OCR esião; Vchiua- begins the example over the row break.
Uchiwa no kenqua and uchiwa no toriai denote internal fighting. The Portuguese Guerra ends with a visible comma before the alternative gloss below.

runs.text: ou briga dos criados, ou ſoldados dalgum capi-

lines.note: The fighting is between servants or soldiers of one captain. The scan joins ſoldados without the OCR’s internal space, and capi- continues below.
Tão completes capitão; the servants or soldiers fight among themselves within one lord’s following. This completes the internal-conflict example.
Uchiwarau means laughing. Caraca- begins the adverb caracarato in the following example, with the visible final a correcting OCR Caraci-.
Rato completes caracarato; vchivarǒte describes laughing loudly. The historical contracted inflection is retained rather than changed to a modern form.
Caquino completes the Portuguese description of loud, cackling laughter. The abraded opening a is retained with the visible surrounding letters; OCR had inserted an additional o.
Uchiwaru means breaking something by striking it. The visible v in the compound is restored against OCR Vchiari.

runs.text: gũa couſa, ou com a mão, &c.

lines.note: The breaking may be done with something or with the hand. Gũa completes the divided algũa and retains its nasal abbreviation.
Uchiwasururu means forgetting. The principal forms ruru and eta reflect the historical inflection stated by the dictionary.
Uchiumi denotes an inlet or arm of the sea. The printed v in Vchivmi represents the compound’s u-vowel and corrects OCR y.
Uchiunataruru means inclining or lowering. The visible v, rather than OCR y, begins the second element; abai- continues into abaixar below.
Cǒbeuo vchivnataruru gives the example of bowing the head. The Portuguese In- begins inclinar on the next row.
Clinar a cabeça completes the explanation of inclining the head. The short line is a real continuation, not furniture.
Uchiunazuku means nodding the head. The following row explains that the nod signals assent or understanding; the Portuguese reads como rather than OCR cemo.

runs.text: quem conſente, ou entende a couſa.

lines.note: The nod is like that of someone agreeing with or understanding a matter. This completes the action described by dar à cabeça.

runs.text: O ir ate porta com al-

lines.note: Uchiokuru denotes accompanying someone to the door or farther. The damaged Portuguese phrase is read O ir ate porta com al-, with porta supported by its remaining strokes and the context. The reading is qualified because the first vowel is abraded; no unprinted article is supplied.

Guem completes alguem: accompanying that person, perhaps farther away. The scan gives acompanhandoo with two final o letters, preserving the attached object pronoun rather than the OCR’s split single-o form.
Uchioku here means leaving or giving up a matter. The principal forms are retained as printed rather than expanded.
Uchioru means breaking a long object. The printed compound begins Vchivori; com- continues as prida on the following page, and the repeated prida at the foot of this page is a catchword.

zones.label: Catchword
zones.note: Repeats the beginning of the next page, completing com-prida across the page turn.
